lesson.text: Quick memory: what is a summary? (A short retelling of the main points, in your own words.) Today you will give a talk. You will also summarise what other speakers say.

Plan a talk. Know your purpose (to inform or to persuade) and your audience. Open with a hook, such as a question or a surprising fact; give two or three main points in order, each with facts; end strongly.
Use cue cards with key words, not every sentence, so you can look at your audience, not your notes. A picture, a chart or a model helps listeners understand and remember your facts.
Listen: a steady pace sounds like these even claps. Speak clearly and loudly enough for the back of the room, at a steady pace. Pause after each main point, so listeners can think.
Look at your audience, stand still and tall, and point to your picture as you talk about it. Practise out loud before the real talk: time yourself, and ask a friend to listen.
Listening is a skill too. As a speaker talks, note the main points and the facts or reasons given for each. Ask yourself: what is the speaker telling me, and how do they back it up?

Summarise a talk in a few sentences: the main points, in your own words, with no small details and nothing the speaker did not say: "Tam said hedgehogs eat slugs, sleep all winter and need gaps in fences."

Try it in the world: give a one-minute talk to your family about a place in your world, with a hook, three facts and a strong ending. Then ask them to summarise it back to you. Next, in grade 6: discussions and presentations.

exercises.prompt: What is a good way to open a talk?
exercises.hint: How can you make listeners want to hear more?
exercises.explain: A hook, such as a question or a surprising fact, catches listeners' attention.
choices: with a question or a surprising fact
with your back to the audience

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a steady pace for a talk?
exercises.hint: Are the claps evenly spaced, and slow enough to follow?
exercises.explain: True: the claps are even and unhurried, like a clear speaker.

exercises.prompt: What should go on cue cards?
exercises.hint: Cue cards are reminders you glance at.
exercises.explain: Key words remind you of each point, so you can look up at your audience.

exercises.prompt: You should look at your audience while you speak.
exercises.hint: How do listeners know you are talking to them?
exercises.explain: True: looking at your audience keeps them listening and shows you are talking to them.

exercises.prompt: What is a summary of a talk?
exercises.hint: A summary is short and keeps only what matters most.
exercises.explain: A summary gives the main points, briefly, in your own words.
choices: the main points, in a few of your words

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a good pace for a talk?
exercises.hint: Could listeners keep up? Are there any pauses?
exercises.explain: False: the words rush out with no pauses, so listeners cannot keep up. Slow down and pause.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of a talk in order.
exercises.hint: Catch the listeners first; leave them with your summary last.
exercises.explain: The hook, the first main point, the second main point, then a strong ending.
items: A hook: a question or surprising fact
A strong ending that sums up

exercises.prompt: A speaker says: "Recycling saves energy. Making cans from old cans uses far less energy than making them from new metal." How does she back up her point?
exercises.hint: What comes after her main point?
exercises.explain: She backs up her point with a fact: recycled cans use far less energy.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: good or poor presenting?
exercises.hint: Which ones help listeners hear, follow and remember?
exercises.explain: Good: speaking clearly, pausing, using a picture. Poor: mumbling, reading every word, rushing.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Where does the speaker pause?
exercises.hint: Listen for the long gap between the claps.
exercises.explain: The claps come in two groups with a gap between: a pause after a main point.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best summary of: "Owls hunt at night. They have silent feathers and sharp hearing, so mice do not hear them coming."?
exercises.hint: Which one keeps every main point, briefly?
exercises.explain: It keeps the main points: night hunting, silent flight and sharp hearing.
choices: Owls hunt silently at night using sharp hearing.

exercises.prompt: Zara says: "We need a school garden. It would teach us how food grows, and bees would have flowers." Which reasons does she give?
exercises.hint: Listen for what comes after her opinion.
exercises.explain: Her two reasons: pupils would learn how food grows, and bees would have flowers.
choices: learning how food grows, and helping bees
it is fun, and it is green

exercises.prompt: Your talk about planets is for young children. What should you do?
exercises.explain: Match your talk to your audience: simple words and pictures for young children.
choices: use simple words and a big picture
use hard words and no pictures

exercises.prompt: A good summary adds new facts that the speaker did not say.
exercises.hint: Whose points does a summary retell?
exercises.explain: False: a summary only retells the speaker's main points; it adds nothing new.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order to prepare a talk.
exercises.hint: You need facts before you can plan, and a plan before cue cards.
exercises.explain: Topic, facts, plan, cue cards, then practise out loud.
items: Plan a hook, points and an ending

exercises.prompt: Tam's talk ends: "So, hedgehogs need our help: leave a gap in your fence!" What kind of ending is this?
exercises.hint: Does it sum up, and does it ask listeners to do something?
exercises.explain: It sums up the talk and gives listeners something to do: a strong ending.
choices: a summary with something to do

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
exercises.hint: Which one catches the audience, like a fish on a hook?
exercises.explain: A hook grabs attention, a cue card holds key words, and a summary retells the main points.

exercises.prompt: Tam's talk about hedgehogs: match each part to his words.
matches: So leave a gap in your fence!
Who here has met a hedgehog?
exercises.hint: A hook grabs attention; a point is backed by a fact; an ending gives listeners something to do.
exercises.explain: The hook is a question: who has met a hedgehog? The main point: hedgehogs help gardeners. The fact: they eat slugs and beetles. The ending: leave a gap in your fence!

exercises.prompt: Tam said hedgehogs eat slugs, sleep all winter and need gaps in fences. Sort the notes for your summary: keep or leave out?
exercises.hint: A summary keeps the main points, and adds nothing the speaker did not say.
exercises.explain: Keep the three main points: slugs, winter sleep and gaps in fences. Leave out details about the talk itself, his jumper and his pauses, and anything Tam never said: hedgehogs cannot fly!
